I'm Sahil, and I've shared a flat with Abhinav for a year. He used to worry out loud all day. The rent. His mother's knee. His appraisal. Whether the landlord would sell the flat.

When the timer beeps, he closes the notebook. If he starts worrying at dinner, he says, "That's for seven o'clock."
I can't tell what's in his head. But he laughs more at dinner now.

"Eshaan, you asked how I got through the year after Nani died. I'm Rekha, and I'm still getting through it, honestly.
She raised me. When she went, in the winter, the house felt hollow. For weeks I couldn't cook, couldn't pray, couldn't do anything.
What helped first was small. Every evening, I lit the brass lamp in front of her photo, the way she did for forty years. It gave the evening a shape. It felt like she was still part of it.
Then my aunt took me to the old-age home where Nani used to volunteer. The women there knew her. They told me stories about her I'd never heard. I started going on Sundays, reading the newspaper to a lady who can't see well.
It doesn't make the missing stop. Some days I still sit on the floor and cry. But helping someone, and lighting the lamp, make it something I can carry."

I've known Nazia since school, and I was with her the week her father died in March.

Shankar, 26, came in on Tuesday with his wife and his older brother. He said, "I'm not coping. I haven't been for months. I thought I could handle it alone."
He described weeks of broken sleep, dreading work and snapping at home. Last Sunday he sat in the car outside his office for an hour, unable to go in. That night he told his wife and brother everything and asked them to help him find someone to talk to.
I told him that noticing his limit and asking for help showed good judgement, not weakness. He seemed surprised. "My father always said men don't need this."

I did it. I told them.
I'm Ankita, and for four months I've been pretending. Going to work, coming home, lying on the bed with the lights off. Not eating much. Crying in the office washroom twice a week. I kept thinking it would pass, that I just needed to try harder.

Akash helped me find a psychologist near the office, and I booked an appointment for Saturday before I could change my mind.
